steps.body: A random variable attaches a NUMBER to each outcome of a chance experiment. Flip three coins and the outcome is a sequence like HTH; the random variable ‘number of heads’ turns that into 2. The experiment supplies the randomness; the variable supplies the arithmetic.
Shade the chance that the variable takes one particular value.

widget.prompt: Three coin flips give 8 equally likely outcomes. Shade the ones where the number of heads is exactly 2.
widget.successFeedback: 3 of 8: HHT, HTH and THH. The random variable takes the value 2 on exactly three outcomes, so P(X = 2) = 3/8.
widget.lowFeedback: Not enough shaded — more than that many outcomes have exactly two heads.
widget.highFeedback: Too much shaded — outcomes with three heads or one head do not belong.

predict.prompt: Three coin flips, X = number of heads. Which values can X take?
predict.reveal: A random variable's possible values are fixed by the experiment: three flips can produce zero through three heads, and nothing else. Listing those values is always the first step, because the distribution has to assign a probability to each one and to nothing more.

explanationVariants: HTH contains two heads, so X = 2 on that outcome.
Count the H's: two of them.

widget.prompt: X counts heads in three flips. What is X for the outcome HTH?

commonErrors.feedback: 3 counts the FLIPS, not the heads. HTH has one tail.
One tail, but two heads — X counts the heads.

widget.fallbackFeedback: HTH has heads in positions 1 and 3, so X = 2.
widget.successFeedback: 2 — the outcome is a sequence, the variable is a number read off it.

steps.body: Several outcomes can share a value, and that is the whole reason expectation is interesting. HHT, HTH and THH are three different outcomes that all give X = 2, so the value 2 collects three shares of probability while X = 3 collects only one. The values are not equally likely even when the outcomes are.

explanationVariants: Only HHH gives three heads, so exactly one outcome has X = 3.
Three heads requires every flip to cooperate — one way.

widget.prompt: How many of the 8 outcomes give X = 3 (three heads)?

commonErrors.feedback: 3 is the VALUE of X, not the number of outcomes producing it. Only HHH does.
8 is every outcome. Most of them contain at least one tail.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Only HHH has three heads, so exactly one outcome gives X = 3.
widget.successFeedback: 1 — which is why X = 3 is far rarer than X = 2, even though both are single values.

explanationVariants: An outcome is what happens; a random variable is the number assigned to it.
HTH is an outcome; 2 is the value the variable gives it.

widget.prompt: Which of these is a random VARIABLE, not an outcome?

options.label: The number of heads in three flips
options.feedback: Yes — it assigns a number to each outcome, which is exactly what a random variable does.

options.label: The sequence HTH
options.feedback: That is one outcome of the experiment. The variable turns it into a number.

options.label: The coin itself
options.feedback: The coin is the apparatus, neither outcome nor variable.

explanationVariants: Rolling two dice, a sum of 7 happens 6 ways out of 36.
The pairs 1-6, 2-5, 3-4, 4-3, 5-2 and 6-1 all sum to 7.
hints: List the ordered pairs whose two faces add to 7.
The first die can be 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6, and the second is then forced.
Every first-die value works exactly once, giving six pairs.

widget.prompt: Roll two dice and let S be their sum. How many of the 36 outcomes give S = 7?

commonErrors.feedback: 7 is the VALUE of S, not the number of ways to reach it.
That counts unordered pairs like {1,6}, {2,5}, {3,4}. The dice are distinguishable, so 1-6 and 6-1 are two outcomes.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Six ordered pairs sum to 7, so 6 of the 36 outcomes give S = 7.
widget.successFeedback: 6 — more than any other sum, which is what makes 7 the centre of that distribution.

takeaways: A random variable assigns a number to each outcome of a chance experiment.
Its possible values are fixed by the experiment and should be listed first.
Several outcomes may share one value, so values are rarely equally likely.
steps.teaser: Next: collect those probabilities into a table — the distribution itself.
